text: I'm Sam. Follow for the next one.
Check the tiny number on the shelf tag. Always.
The full story's on my channel. It gets worse.
Send this to someone who'd pick up that call.
Slow down. Every scam needs you to hurry.

Your bank will never ask you to do this one thing. Move your money to keep it safe. That's the line. A caller says there's fraud on your account, they sound calm, they know your name, maybe the last four digits of your card. And then they say: to protect your savings, move it to a new account we've set up. That new account is theirs. Real fraud teams freeze money. They don't move it. If anyone asks you to move money to protect it, hang up, and call the number on the back of your card.

Same price. Four fewer ounces. A few years ago, a big sports-drink brand quietly switched its bottle from thirty-two ounces to twenty-eight. Same shelf, same price, slightly different shape. That's shrinkflation. Instead of raising the price, a company shrinks what's inside, and hopes you won't notice. Chips, toilet paper, ice cream, cereal. The fix is the tiny unit price on the shelf tag. Price per ounce doesn't lie, even when the box does.

Calling your bank back can still connect you to the scammer. Here's how. They call you, pretending to be your bank, and say: hang up and call the number on your card, to be safe. You hang up. But on some landlines, if the caller doesn't hang up, the line stays open. You dial, you hear a ring, and the same person picks up. On a landline, wait a full minute or use a different phone. On a cell, you're fine. And remember, the real bank rarely tells you to call it back right now.

You don't owe four dollars and fifteen cents in tolls. That text, the one that says your unpaid toll will turn into a big fine unless you pay today, is one of the most common scams in America right now. The amount is small on purpose, so you don't think twice. The link goes to a fake payment page that takes your card details. Real toll agencies don't text you a link to pay. If you're worried, go to the toll agency's site by typing the address yourself. Then delete the text.

Look at the space between the peaks. A famous triangle-shaped chocolate bar once made a bar lighter by spreading out the triangles. Same length, same box, but wide gaps where chocolate used to be. People noticed, because the gaps were hard to miss. Most shrinkflation is harder to see. A deeper dent in the bottom of a jar. A bigger air gap in a bag. Fewer sheets on a roll. Companies count on you to look at the package, not the weight.

This tracking link is the package. You get a text: your delivery couldn't be completed, update your address here. You probably are expecting something. Everyone is. That's why it works. The link takes you to a page that looks like the delivery company and asks for a small redelivery fee. What they want is your card number. Delivery companies don't text random links asking for money. Track packages in the app you ordered from, or the carrier's own app. Not in a text from a number you don't know.

The voice sounded exactly like her grandson. It wasn't him. He was crying, he'd been in an accident, he needed bail money, and please, don't tell Mom. Scammers can now copy a voice from a few seconds of video posted online. The giveaway isn't the voice. It's the secret and the hurry. Make a family code word today, something only you would know. If the call ever comes, ask for it. And hang up and call the person directly on their own number. It takes thirty seconds.

The most important number in the store is the tiny one. On most shelf tags, there's a big price, and a small one in the corner: the unit price. Price per ounce, per count, per hundred sheets. That's the only fair way to compare. The family size isn't always cheaper. The sale pack isn't always a deal. Two seconds of reading the small number can save you more than any coupon.

No real company has ever asked to be paid in gift cards. Not the IRS. Not your power company. Not tech support. Not the police. Gift cards are how scammers get paid because once you read them the numbers on the back, the money is gone, and it's almost impossible to trace. If anyone asks you to buy gift cards and read them the numbers, it's a scam. Every time. Some cashiers now warn people at the register, and they've stopped a lot of these. Be the person who listens.

The job paid forty-five dollars an hour, work from home, no interview needed. That was the problem. Fake job offers are exploding. First they hire you over text or chat. Then they need your bank details for payroll. Or they send you a check to buy equipment, and ask you to send the extra back. Or they ask you to pay a small fee to unlock your earnings. Real employers interview you. They don't pay you before you start, and they never ask you to pay them.

Joining the gym took two minutes. Quitting takes a certified letter. Some gyms make cancelling deliberately painful. In person only. Mailed letter only. Thirty days' notice, plus an annual fee you forgot about. It's not an accident. Every month you don't cancel is money. Before you sign up, ask one question: how do I cancel? Get the answer in writing. And new rules in some states now say if you can join online, you must be able to cancel online.

They sent you too much money on purpose. You sell something online. The buyer sends a check for more than the price, and asks you to send back the difference. The check clears in your account, so you send the money. A week later the check bounces, because it was fake, and the bank takes all of it back from you. Banks make deposits available fast, but that doesn't mean the check is real. Never send back overpayments. Ever.

He was perfect for eight months. Then came the crypto. Romance scams are patient. They meet you online, they message every day, they're kind and attentive, and they can never quite video call. Then, one day, they mention an investment that's made them rich. They'll show you how. Or they have an emergency and need help. People have lost their life savings this way. If someone you've never met in person brings up money, stop. Show the messages to a friend. Scammers hate a second opinion.

The store makes more money on this than on the TV. The extended warranty. On many electronics, the profit margin on the TV itself is thin. The protection plan is where the money is. Most electronics that fail do it in the first year, while they're still covered by the maker's warranty. And many credit cards add an extra year for free. Before you say yes at the register, check what you already have.

Scammers have a name for you, and it isn't nice. They call it pig butchering. First they fatten the pig. A friendly wrong-number text becomes a friendship. They show you a trading app where their investments are soaring, and they help you put in a little. You see big gains. You put in more. Then you try to take money out, and there's a fee, then a tax, then the app disappears. The gains were never real. If a stranger is teaching you to invest, you are the investment.

Your computer is fine. The phone number isn't. A loud warning pops up, maybe with an alarm sound, saying your computer is infected and you need to call support right now. It's just a web page. It can't see your computer. The people on that number will ask to remote into your machine, then charge you to fix a problem that doesn't exist, or empty your bank account while they're in there. Close the browser. If it won't close, restart the computer. Never call a number in a pop-up.

The room was a hundred and twenty-nine dollars. The bill was a hundred and seventy-eight. Resort fees, destination fees, amenity fees. Charged per night, for things like the gym and the Wi-Fi you didn't use, added at the end. They let hotels advertise a lower price than you'll actually pay. Newer US rules now push hotels to show the full price up front. But always check the total before you click book.

The buyer wants to pay you too fast. You list something online. A buyer messages instantly, doesn't ask any questions, and wants to pay with an app right now. Then you get an email saying the payment is pending until you upgrade to a business account, or send a small fee. That email isn't from the payment app. Real payments show up in the app itself, not in an email. Meet in person, check the app, and never pay anything to receive money.

The apartment was real. The landlord wasn't. Scammers copy real rental listings, lower the price so it's a great deal, and post them again. They can't show it in person right now, they're out of town. But send the deposit and first month's rent, and they'll mail you the keys. The keys never come. The real owner has no idea. Never pay for a place you haven't seen inside, with the person who can actually open the door. Look up who owns it. It's often public.

A nine hundred dollar TV for three thousand dollars. That's rent-to-own. No credit check, just small weekly payments. Twenty-five dollars a week sounds easy. But keep paying for two years, and you've paid three times the price. Miss a few, and they take it back, and you keep nothing. If you can, save for a few weeks and buy it outright, or buy used. It's almost always the expensive way to buy something cheap.

Look closely at that sticker on the parking meter. Scammers have been putting fake QR codes on parking meters and pay stations, right over the real ones. You scan it, it opens a payment page, it looks normal, and you just gave a stranger your card. Before you scan a code in public, touch it. If it's a sticker on top of another sticker, walk away. Use the city's official parking app, or pay at the machine.

The IRS doesn't call. It mails a letter. A caller says you owe back taxes and police are on the way unless you pay right now, with a gift card or a wire. That isn't how it works. The IRS usually contacts you by mail first, it never demands a specific payment type, and it can't have you arrested over the phone. If you're worried, hang up and look up your account on the official IRS website yourself.

Four easy payments. One hard lesson. Buy now, pay later makes everything feel cheaper. Two hundred dollars becomes fifty. But stack a few of them, and suddenly four different payments are hitting your account on the same week. Miss one, and there can be late fees. People use it for groceries now. It's not free money. It's a loan with a friendly button. Add up every one you have open before you tap again.

Your Social Security number can't be suspended. That's the whole scam. A recorded voice says your number has been suspended because of suspicious activity, press one. Then a person asks you to confirm your number, or pay to fix it. Social Security numbers don't get suspended. The agency won't threaten you, and it won't ask for payment by gift card or crypto. Hang up. If you want to check, call Social Security on the number from its official website.

Pay in thirty minutes or your power goes out. It won't. This one targets small businesses: restaurants at dinner rush, shops on a Saturday. A caller says they're from the utility, you're behind, and a crew is on the way. Pay now by app or gift card. Real utilities send notices for weeks before cutting anyone off. They don't send a crew in thirty minutes. Hang up and call the number on your bill.

The thirty-five dollar cup of coffee. Your account is a few dollars short. You buy a five-dollar latte. The bank approves it, then charges an overdraft fee that can be around thirty-five dollars. Some banks charge that per purchase, per day. Turn off overdraft coverage for debit cards. Then a short account just declines the card. Mildly embarrassing. Much cheaper. Or switch to one of the banks that don't charge overdraft fees at all.

The refund link costs more than the product. You get an email or text: your product has been recalled, click here for a refund. Or, you were overcharged, we owe you money. The page asks for your card details to send the refund. Refunds don't need your card number. Real recalls are listed on government safety websites, and real refunds go back to the card you already used. If someone needs your card to give you money, they're taking it.

Sorry, wrong number. That's how it starts. A friendly text from a stranger: is this Dr. Lee? Oh, sorry. But you seem nice. They chat. They send pictures. They're charming. A few weeks later, it's crypto or an emergency. These texts are sent to thousands of people at once, hoping a few reply. Don't reply, not even to say wrong number. Replying tells them your number is real and you're polite. Block it and move on.

Your price changed while you were looking. Dynamic pricing means the price adjusts in real time. Flights, hotels, concert tickets, ride shares. Demand goes up, the price goes up. Some sites may also show different prices to different people. So compare in a private browser window, check on a different device, and if you can wait, wait. Sometimes the best way to get a lower price is just not to look so interested.

The trial was free. The fourteenth month wasn't. Free trials are designed for you to forget. They need your card, they renew automatically, and the cancel button is hard to find. Some scam trials are worse: one small shipping fee that quietly signs you up for a monthly charge from a company you can't contact. Before you start any trial, put a reminder in your phone for the day before it ends. And check your card statement every month. Line by line.

After a disaster, real charities don't text you a link. Every hurricane, wildfire or earthquake brings a wave of fake charities, with names that sound almost right. They text, they call, they post photos of victims. Your money goes nowhere good. Give directly through a charity's own website, one you typed in yourself. Check it on a charity rating site first. And be wary of anyone who wants a donation in gift cards, wire transfers or crypto.

Nitrogen in the tires: a hundred and ninety-nine dollars. Car dealer add-ons are where a lot of the profit is. Paint protection. VIN etching. Fabric coating. Nitrogen. Often added to the paperwork before you see it, often almost worthless. The air we breathe is already mostly nitrogen. Ask for an itemized out-the-door price before you sit down to sign anything, and cross out every add-on you didn't ask for.

Wiggle the card reader at the gas pump first. Skimmers are fake card readers that fit right over the real one. They copy your card while you fill up. Some have tiny cameras to catch your PIN. Grab the reader and give it a tug. If it moves, or looks different from the pump next to it, don't use it. Better yet, pay with tap or your phone, which skimmers can't copy the same way, or pay inside.

Your car's warranty isn't expiring. Your patience is. Those calls about your extended auto warranty are robocalls selling overpriced service contracts, or just trying to get your personal information. Some use the name of your car's maker. They're not the maker. Don't press one to be removed. That just confirms someone answers. Hang up, block the number, and add yourself to the national Do Not Call list. If you want a warranty, call the dealer you actually bought the car from.

The milk is in the back of the store for a reason. The things you buy every week, milk, eggs, bread, are usually spread out far from the door. So to get them, you walk past everything else. Fresh flowers and bakery smells at the entrance. Candy at the register. End-of-aisle displays that look like deals but often aren't. Go in with a list. Shop the edges. And never shop hungry.

A company wired twenty-five million dollars to a deepfake. An employee at a big firm joined a video call with his finance chief and several colleagues. They asked him to make a series of transfers. He did. Every other person on that call was fake, generated by AI. This is coming to smaller businesses and families too. The fix is old-fashioned. If anyone asks for money on a call, hang up and call them back on a number you already know.

Here's the one rule that beats almost every scam. Slow down. Every scam needs you to hurry. Your account is frozen. Your grandson is in jail. Your power goes off in thirty minutes. The deal ends tonight. Urgency is the trick, because when you're rushed, you stop checking. So give yourself permission to take ten minutes. Hang up. Call someone you trust. Look it up yourself. A real problem will still be there in ten minutes. A scam won't.

It was never eighty-nine dollars. That big crossed-out price above the sale price is called an anchor. It makes thirty-nine look like a steal. But sometimes the item was barely ever sold at the higher price, or not at all. Stores test how high an anchor they can get away with. Ignore the crossed-out number. Ask yourself one thing: would I pay thirty-nine dollars for this if there was no sale? That's the real price.

There's no warrant out for you because you missed jury duty. The caller says they're a deputy. They know your name and address. You missed a jury summons, there's a warrant, and you can clear it by paying a fine right now. Courts don't call to collect fines over the phone, and they never take gift cards or crypto. If you're worried, look up your county court's number yourself and call. They'll be happy to tell you there's nothing.

Did you order a nine hundred and ninety-nine dollar iPhone? No. Neither did they. You get a call or text saying a big order was placed on your account, press one to cancel. The person who answers needs to verify you, so they ask for your login, or to remote into your computer, or for a code they just texted you. That code is the key to your account. Check your orders in the app yourself. There's nothing there.

You're probably paying for subscriptions you forgot about. Surveys keep finding that people underestimate what they spend on subscriptions, often by a lot. A streaming service you tried for one show. An app with a free trial. Cloud storage. Each one is small, which is exactly why they last. Once a year, sit down with your bank statement and look for every monthly charge. Cancel anything you didn't use last month.

Nobody legitimate will ever ask you to use a bitcoin ATM. Not the bank, not the government, not the police. But scammers love them. They keep you on the phone, send you to a gas station or a convenience store, and walk you through feeding cash into a crypto kiosk. Once it's in, it's gone. If someone on the phone is guiding you to one of these machines, hang up. Then tell someone what just happened.

Did you just try to spend twelve hundred dollars? Reply yes or no. That text isn't from your bank. You reply no. Seconds later, someone calls from what looks like your bank's number, and walks you through securing your account. Which really means sending money to them, or reading them a code. Caller ID can be faked. Your bank's real fraud alerts will never ask you to move money or share a code. Call the number on your card.

If you pay cash, you might be paying for someone else's credit card rewards. Every time someone swipes a card, the store pays a fee, often two or three percent. Many stores just raise their prices for everyone to cover it. So the person paying cash pays the higher price, and gets no points. Studies have found rewards flow toward wealthier households. Not a scam, exactly. Just a hidden transfer.

The concert tickets were half price. They didn't exist. A post in a fan group: I can't go anymore, selling two tickets at face value. They send a screenshot of the tickets, ask you to pay by a payment app as friends and family, and then they vanish. Sometimes they sell the same screenshot to twenty people. Buy tickets through the official seller or a resale site with buyer protection. Never pay a stranger as a friend.

The puppy was perfect. It was a stock photo. Pet scams are some of the most heartbreaking online. A cute puppy, a great price, a breeder who's far away. Pay a deposit, then a shipping fee, then a special crate, then insurance. The puppy never comes. Search the photos online to see if they show up elsewhere. Insist on a video call with the puppy. Better still, visit a local shelter or a breeder you can meet in person.

Why is the self-checkout screen asking you for a tip? Tipping screens are everywhere now, with eighteen, twenty and twenty-five percent already selected. They turn the screen toward you while the cashier watches. That pressure is the design. Tipping for table service is one thing. You're allowed to tap no tip, or custom, for a muffin someone handed you. Decide what you think is fair before the screen spins around.

You won a car, or a hundred thousand dollars. Just pay the taxes and fees first, and we'll send your prize. That's how you know it's fake. Real prizes don't ask you to pay to collect them. Real sweepstakes take any taxes out of the prize, or you settle them with the government yourself later. And if you didn't enter, you didn't win. There's no prize. There's only the fee.

Never read anyone the code that was just texted to you. Not the bank, not tech support, not a friend in a panic. That six-digit code is the second lock on your account. A scammer already has your password, or is resetting it, and the code is the last thing they need. They'll say they're sending it to verify you. They're not. The message itself usually says: never share this code. Believe the text, not the voice.

One mega roll equals four regular rolls. Sometimes. Toilet paper and paper towel packs are some of the hardest things in the store to compare. Double, mega, super mega, ultra. Each brand defines a regular roll differently. And the number of sheets per roll has been quietly drifting down. Ignore the names on the package. Look for total sheets, or the price per hundred sheets on the shelf tag. That's the only honest number.

Student loan forgiveness doesn't cost four hundred and ninety-nine dollars. Companies call and text saying they can get your loans wiped out, for a fee. Some ask for your federal student aid login, then change your contact details so you don't see what they're doing. Everything they offer you can do yourself, for free, on the official federal student aid website. Never give anyone your login. Never pay to apply for forgiveness.
